_**User (2026-11-20 00:53:46Z)**_

Review target: `196`

`high effort → 8 inline angles → dedup (no verify) → ≤10 findings`

You are reviewing for **recall** at high effort: catch every real bug a careful
reviewer would catch in one sitting. At this level, catching real bugs matters
more than avoiding false positives. Err on the side of surfacing.

## Phase 0 — Gather the diff

Run `git diff @{upstream}...HEAD` (or `git diff main...HEAD` / `git diff HEAD~1`
if there's no upstream) to get the unified diff under review. If there are
uncommitted changes, or the range diff is empty, also run `git diff HEAD` and
include the working-tree changes in scope — the review often runs before the
commit. If a PR number, branch name, or file path was passed as an argument,
review that target instead. Treat this diff as the review scope.

## Phase 1 — Find candidates (3 correctness angles + 3 cleanup angles + 1 altitude angle + 1 conventions angle, up to 6 each)

Run **8 independent finder angles** in sequence yourself, in THIS context — do NOT spawn subagents for them. Each
surfaces **up to 6 candidate findings** with `file`, `line`, a one-line
`summary`, and a concrete `failure_scenario`.

### Angle A — line-by-line diff scan

Read every hunk in the diff, line by line. Then Read the enclosing function for
each hunk — bugs in unchanged lines of a touched function are in scope (the PR
re-exposes or fails to fix them). For every line ask: what input, state, timing,
or platform makes this line wrong? Look for inverted/wrong conditions,
off-by-one, null/undefined deref, missing `await`, falsy-zero checks,
wrong-variable copy-paste, error swallowed in catch, unescaped regex metachars.

### Angle B — removed-behavior auditor

For every line the diff DELETES or replaces, name the invariant or behavior it
enforced, then search the new code for where that invariant is re-established.
If you can't find it, that's a candidate: a removed guard, a dropped error
path, a narrowed validation, a deleted test that was covering a real case.

### Angle C — cross-file tracer

For each function the diff changes, find its callers (Grep for the symbol) and
check whether the change breaks any call site: a new precondition, a changed
return shape, a new exception, a timing/ordering dependency. Also check callees:
does a parallel change in the same PR make a call unsafe?

### Reuse

The angles above hunt for bugs; this one and the next two hunt for cleanup in
the changed code. Flag new code that re-implements something the codebase
already has — Grep shared/utility modules and files adjacent to the change,
and name the existing helper to call instead.

### Simplification

Flag unnecessary complexity the diff adds: redundant or derivable state,
copy-paste with slight variation, deep nesting, dead code left behind. Name
the simpler form that does the same job.

### Efficiency

Flag wasted work the diff introduces: redundant computation or repeated I/O,
independent operations run sequentially, blocking work added to startup or
hot paths. Also flag long-lived objects built from closures or captured
environments — they keep the entire enclosing scope alive for the object's
lifetime (a memory leak when that scope holds large values); prefer a
class/struct that copies only the fields it needs. Name the cheaper
alternative.

### Altitude

Check that each change fixes the root cause at the right depth rather than
patching a symptom with a fragile bandaid. Special cases layered on shared
infrastructure are a sign the fix isn't deep enough — prefer the simpler, more
general change to the underlying mechanism over adding special cases, and name
that change.

### Conventions (CLAUDE.md)

Find the CLAUDE.md files that govern the changed code: the user-level
~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, the repo-root CLAUDE.md, plus any CLAUDE.md or
CLAUDE.local.md in a directory that is an ancestor of a changed file (a
directory's CLAUDE.md only applies to files at or below it). Read each one
that exists, then check the diff for clear violations of the rules they state.

Only flag a violation when you can quote the exact rule and the exact line
that breaks it — no style preferences, no vague "spirit of the doc"
inferences. In the finding, name the CLAUDE.md path and quote the rule so the
report can cite it. If no CLAUDE.md applies, return nothing for this angle.

Cleanup, altitude, and conventions candidates use the same
`file`/`line`/`summary` shape; in `failure_scenario`, state the concrete
cost (what is duplicated, wasted, harder to maintain, or which CLAUDE.md rule
is broken) instead of a crash. Correctness bugs always outrank cleanup,
altitude, and conventions findings when the output cap forces a cut.

Pass every candidate with a nameable failure scenario through — finders that
silently drop half-believed candidates are the dominant cause of misses.

## Phase 2 — Dedup only (no verify)

Pool all candidates. Dedup near-duplicates only (same defect, same location, same reason → keep one). Do NOT run verifiers; do NOT re-judge. Sort by severity.

## Output

Target **at least 5 findings**. If fewer genuine findings exist, emit what you have — do not invent to hit the floor.

Call the ReportFindings tool once to report this review's results
with `{level, findings}`. `findings` is at most 10 entries ranked
most-severe first; each entry has `file`, `line`, `summary`,
`short_summary` — the claim compressed to ≤60 characters, no rationale
or consequence clause — `failure_scenario`, and `category` — a short kebab-case slug for the angle
that produced it (`correctness`, `simplification`, `efficiency`,
`reuse`, `altitude`, `conventions`, or a more specific slug like
`test-coverage` when one fits better) — plus `verdict` when a verify pass
produced one. If more than 10 survive, keep the 10 most severe. If
nothing survives, call it with an empty array. Do not also print
the findings as text, and do not create or publish an artifact of the review -
the tool call is the report.


## If findings are fixed later

Whenever reported findings get fixed later in this session - the user asks you
to fix them, or later work fixes them incidentally - you MUST call ReportFindings again with the same findings, each
carrying an `outcome`: `fixed`, `no_change_needed` (the finding was wrong or
already handled), or `skipped` (real but not applied). Do not repeat the
findings as text.
Make that call immediately after the fixes land, before any prose summary; the
host UI's per-finding status updates only from it, and without it the findings
stay marked unresolved.

// applySuggestionToContent replaces line lineNum (1-based) of content with the suggestion's lines, the way
// #154 draws the diff: "" deletes the line, "\n" leaves one blank line, otherwise one line per suggestion line.
// original is the line the suggestion was written against, and above the lines the reviewer saw right above it;
// content and both of those may use CRLF.
func applySuggestionToContent(content string, lineNum int, above []string, original, suggestion string) (string, error) {
	lines := strings.SplitAfter(content, "\n") // every element but the last keeps its "\n"
	if lines[len(lines)-1] == "" {
		lines = lines[:len(lines)-1] // content ended with a newline
	}
	idx := lineNum - 1
	if idx < len(above) || idx >= len(lines) { // also refuses lineNum < 1, and a line that moved too near the top
		return "", ErrSuggestionOutdated
	}
	// blame-based invalidation misses a line that moved onto an identical one, like another "}"; its neighbours don't
	for i, want := range above {
		if strings.TrimSuffix(strings.TrimSuffix(lines[idx-len(above)+i], "\n"), "\r") != strings.TrimSuffix(want, "\r") {
			return "", ErrSuggestionOutdated
		}
	}

	target := lines[idx]
	ending := ""
	switch {
	case strings.HasSuffix(target, "\r\n"):
		ending = "\r\n"
	case strings.HasSuffix(target, "\n"):
		ending = "\n"
	}
	if strings.TrimSuffix(target, ending) != strings.TrimSuffix(original, "\r") {
		return "", ErrSuggestionOutdated
	}

	var replacement string
	if suggestion != "" {
		innerEnding := ending
		if innerEnding == "" { // the last line has no newline, so new lines in between take the file's own
			innerEnding = "\n"
			if strings.Contains(content, "\r\n") {
				innerEnding = "\r\n"
			}
		}
		newLines := strings.Split(strings.TrimSuffix(suggestion, "\n"), "\n")
		replacement = strings.Join(newLines, innerEnding) + ending
	}

	before := strings.Join(lines[:idx], "")
	if replacement == "" && ending == "" && idx > 0 {
		// deleting a last line that has no newline: the line before it becomes last and loses its newline,
		// so the file still ends without one (#156 AC11)
		prev := lines[idx-1]
		before = strings.Join(lines[:idx-1], "") + strings.TrimSuffix(strings.TrimSuffix(prev, "\n"), "\r")
	}
	result := before + replacement + strings.Join(lines[idx+1:], "")
	if result == content {
		return "", ErrSuggestionNoChange
	}
	return result, nil
}

// ApplySuggestion commits a review comment's suggestion to the pull request's head branch (#156)
func ApplySuggestion(ctx *context.Context) {
	form := web.GetForm(ctx).(*forms.ApplySuggestionForm)
	issue := GetActionIssue(ctx)
	if ctx.Written() {
		return
	}
	if !issue.IsPull {
		ctx.NotFound(nil)
		return
	}
	if ctx.HasError() {
		ctx.JSONError(ctx.GetErrMsg())
		return
	}
	comment, err := issues_model.GetCommentByID(ctx, ctx.PathParamInt64("id"))
	if issues_model.IsErrCommentNotExist(err) {
		ctx.NotFound(err)
		return
	} else if err != nil {
		ctx.ServerError("GetCommentByID", err)
		return
	}
	if err := issue.LoadPullRequest(ctx); err != nil {
		ctx.ServerError("LoadPullRequest", err)
		return
	}

	err = files_service.ApplySuggestion(ctx, ctx.Doer, issue.PullRequest, comment, form.HeadCommitID, form.Message)
	if err != nil {
		applySuggestionError(ctx, issue.PullRequest.HeadBranch, err)
		return
	}
	ctx.JSONOK() // the page reloads to show the new commit
}

// SuggestionOriginalLine returns the commented line as the reviewer saw it: the last line of the
// stored patch, since CutDiffAroundLine stops right after the commented line.
// For a multi-line comment it returns every line of the range, joined by "\n".
// Old-side comments return None until #151 decides whether they may carry suggestions.
func (c *Comment) SuggestionOriginalLine() optional.Option[string] {
	if c.Type != CommentTypeCode || c.Line <= 0 {
		return optional.None[string]()
	}
	if c.RangeStartLine() > 0 {
		lines, ok := c.RangeOriginalLines()
		if !ok {
			return optional.None[string]()
		}
		return optional.Some(strings.Join(lines, "\n"))
	}
	patch := strings.TrimRight(c.Patch, "\n")
	last := patch[strings.LastIndexByte(patch, '\n')+1:]
	if last == "" || (last[0] != '+' && last[0] != ' ') {
		return optional.None[string]() // "-" is the other side; "@", "d", "\\" mean no code line
	}
	return optional.Some(last[1:])
}

// RangeOriginalLines returns lines RangeStartLine..Line of a multi-line code comment as the
// reviewer saw them, false if the stored patch doesn't hold all of them.
func (c *Comment) RangeOriginalLines() ([]string, bool) {
	start := c.RangeStartLine()
	if start <= 0 || c.Line < start {
		return nil, false
	}
	return PatchLastNewLines(c.Patch, int(c.Line-start+1))
}

	rows := strings.Split(strings.TrimRight(patch, "\n"), "\n")
	lines := make([]string, n)

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-11-20 00:55:36Z)**_

I reviewed PR #196 (#159, applying several suggestions as one commit) and found 7 issues. Nothing has been posted to GitHub and no code was changed.

**The two that matter most:**

1. **The batch button breaks on older browsers.** [suggestion.ts:177](web_src/js/markup/suggestion.ts) calls `.some()` directly on a Map's values (`batch.values().some(...)`). That's a newer JavaScript feature (ES2025), but the build targets es2020 and doesn't polyfill it. On Safari before 18.4 or Firefox before 131, adding a second suggestion to the batch throws an error, so batches of more than one never work there. Copying into an array first (`[...batch.values()].some(...)`) or using a plain `for…of` loop fixes it.
2. **A deleted or edited comment can get stuck in the batch.** If a comment is deleted after being added, or edited so it no longer has exactly one suggestion, it stays in the batch but its Add/Remove button is gone. Every "Apply suggestions" then fails with a bare 404 and the generic "An error occurred" until the page is reloaded.

**Smaller issues:**

3. **Some batch errors don't say which suggestion failed.** A suggestion that can't be applied, or a missing comment, comes back as an unnamed 404, and an overlap error doesn't name the pair. Outdated, already-applied and no-change errors do name the suggestion.
4. **Count label:** the selected count is built by joining strings, so one suggestion reads "1 suggestions selected", and translators can't reorder the number or choose plural forms.
5. **Error suffix:** the " (path:line)" part is added after translation, so other languages can't place or punctuate it themselves.
6. **Loading speed:** comments are loaded one database query per ID, plus another for each one's review and another for each one's author. A full batch of 50 is about 150 queries before any git work starts.
7. **Repeated template code:** about 11 new `data-*` attributes are copied into both `comments.tmpl` and `conversation.tmpl`. The next change has to be made in both places or the two tabs will behave differently.

The service-layer logic looked right: applying bottom-up, the overlap check, the protected-branch check for each file, and crediting each reviewer once. The tests cover every acceptance criterion from AC1 to AC14.

## Code review rubric

The reviewer posts this as a **PR comment**, as well as the GitHub review itself. A copy-paste copy
is in `.github/code-review-rubric.md`, so keep the two in sync. Pull the branch and test it when you
can, say what you checked, and mark each point as required or optional
(`docs/community-governance.md`). Score each row against the issue's acceptance criteria. Anything
below 7 needs a note saying what would raise it.

```markdown

**Checked:** <what you ran or tried>

| Criterion | Score (1–10) | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Correctness — implements issue requirements | | |
| Test coverage — tests present and meaningful | | |
| Test evidence — does every AC have a test? Are the expected values justified? Which tests did you run locally? | | |
| Code quality — style, naming, no duplication | | |
| Documentation — comments and PR description clear | | |
| AI transparency — evidence of human verification if AI used | | |
| Overall — merge as-is? | | |
```

## Mutation testing (D6)

A mutation testing tool makes small changes to the code (*mutants*), such as flipping a condition
or a boundary value, and runs the tests against each one. If a test fails, the mutant is
**killed**. If every test passes, it **survived**: the tests didn't notice the change, which points
to a weak or missing test. An **equivalent** mutant behaves exactly like the original code, so no
test can kill it. Definitions are in the course Glossary.

**Which issue:** one of your issues whose PR changes source code and tests (CSCI 535: two, and the
small issue may be one of them). A tool is required; mutating code by hand doesn't count.

| Code changed | Tool |
| --- | --- |
| Frontend TypeScript (Vitest) | StrykerJS with the Vitest runner |
| Go backend | Gremlins or go-mutesting |

1. Run the tool on the **source files changed by your PR(s)** for that issue, not the whole
   project.
2. Analyse every surviving mutant: equivalent, or a gap in your tests? If more than 10 survive,
   analyse at least 10, starting with lines your PR added or changed.
3. Add or strengthen **at least one test that kills a survivor** that revealed a gap, and re-run
   the tool to confirm it is killed. If no survivor reveals a gap (all killed or equivalent), say so
   and justify it in the surviving-mutants table; that completes this step.
4. Answer the three questions in the write-up.

Files:

```text
feat(pull): apply several suggestions in one commit (#159) Jack-Donohue b14a4a3640bed446b9cad05c53d4bcd796707735 open False
Closes #159

## What changed

A PR author can now pick several suggestions and apply them as one commit. Each suggestion that has an Apply button also gets **Add to batch**. Once something is in the batch, a bar at the bottom of the page shows "N suggestions selected", an editable commit message and **Apply suggestions**.

- **Service (`services/repository/files/suggestion.go`):** new `ApplySuggestions(ctx, doer, pr, comments, expectedHeadSHA, message)`. S3's `ApplySuggestion` is now a one-element call to it, so single Apply runs the same checks and keeps #156's and #157's messages.
  - Before anything is committed, it checks:
    - the batch size (at most 50) and duplicate IDs;
    - each comment's S3 checks and S4's already-applied check;
    - push permission and the head commit (once for the batch);
    - branch protection (per file);
    - outdated comments.
  - It reads each file once, applies that file's suggestions bottom-up so earlier edits don't shift later line numbers, and refuses two suggestions that share a line. Then it makes one `ChangeRepoFiles` commit with one entry per file, and marks every suggestion applied with that commit (S4's `MarkSuggestionApplied`; a failed save is logged, as in S4).
  - Default message: one suggestion keeps S3's "Apply suggestion from @x on file"; several get "Apply N suggestions from code review". Each reviewer other than the applier gets one `Co-authored-by` trailer.
  - A refusal caused by one suggestion is wrapped in `ErrSuggestionAt`, so the page can say which one, e.g. "… already been applied. (README.md:4)".
- **Web:**
  - New route `POST …/files/reviews/comments/apply` that takes `comment_ids`, `head_commit_id` and `message`, reusing S3's form.
  - New `ApplySuggestions` handler. It refuses more than 50 IDs before looking any of them up, so a long list can't cost a query per ID.
  - `applySuggestionError` maps the new errors to 400s and appends `(path:line)` for a named suggestion.
  - New locale strings.
- **Templates:** the two comment templates add the batch data attributes inside the existing Apply condition, so a suggestion with no Apply (no push access, closed PR, outdated, already applied, a range) gets no batch button either. The limit comes from `files_service.MaxSuggestionBatch`.
- **Frontend (`web_src/js/markup/suggestion.ts`):**
  - **Add to batch / Remove from batch** sits next to Apply, and keeps its label when an edited comment is re-rendered.
  - The batch is held only in the page.
  - An overlapping suggestion, or a 51st, is refused with a toast.
  - The bottom bar posts the batch and reloads.
  - S3's POST-and-reload code moved into a shared `postApply`.
- **Merge with `main`:** S4 (#157) landed in the same function while this was open. Its already-applied check now lives in the per-suggestion checks, and its marking runs for every suggestion in the commit.

## Why

Applying suggestions one at a time adds a commit per suggestion. #159 asks for one commit. This covers #159 AC1–AC14. AC15 (a range suggestion in a batch) waits for #189, which makes ranges applicable.

**Not tested automatically, and why:** AC15 isn't implemented in this PR (see Tech Debt). Every implemented AC has an automated test.

**Mutation testing (D6):** [`docs/sprint3/mutation/159-Jack-Donohue.md`](docs/sprint3/mutation/159-Jack-Donohue.md). StrykerJS on this PR's lines of `suggestion.ts`: 89.55% → 96.27%. Five new tests kill the nine survivors that showed gaps.

None were copied from output. When an integration subtest first failed, it was because I had used the wrong line numbers; the server had done what the test asked, so the line numbers were fixed in the test, not the expected file. The re-render test was checked by removing its fix and seeing it fail.

## CI / manual verification

The full suites take hours locally, so I ran the targeted ones after merging `main`; CI runs the rest.

- `go test ./services/repository/files/ ./routers/web/repo/ ./models/issues/`: pass.
- `go test -run '^(TestPullReviewApplySuggestions|TestPullReviewApplySuggestion|TestPullReviewRangeComment|TestPullReviewSuggestionAttribute|TestAPIPullReviewSuggestionRenders)$' gitea.dev/tests/integration` (SQLite): pass.
- `pnpm exec vitest run web_src/js/markup web_src/js/features/repo-diff`: 50 passed.
- `GITEA_TEST_E2E_TIMEOUT_FACTOR=4 GITEA_TEST_E2E_FLAGS='tests/e2e/pr-suggest-change.test.ts --workers=1' make test-e2e`: 12 passed (4 tests × Chromium, Firefox, WebKit).
- `golangci-lint run` on the changed packages: 0 issues. `vue-tsc`, `eslint`, `gofmt` and `./.claude-students/check.sh`: clean.

## Design

See the Design Decision in #159. There is one `ChangeRepoFiles` call per batch, and each file's suggestions are applied bottom-up. S3's single Apply goes through the same function, so S4's applied check and marking cover both.

## Tech Debt

**Introduced:**

- AC15 waits for #189. Until then, range suggestions have no Apply and no batch button.
- The two comment templates now carry eleven more `data-suggestion-*` attributes each. A shared subtemplate would keep them in step (also noted in the #179 review).
- The bar's default message "Apply N suggestions from code review" is written in both `suggestion.go` and `suggestion.ts`.
- The "N suggestions selected" label is a count followed by a locale string, with no plural form.

**Encountered:**

- Commenting on a line past the end of a file returns a 500 (the `isErrBlameNotFoundOrNotEnoughLines` issue already listed in #177's Tech Debt). I hit it while writing the integration test.

=====ISSUE
S6. Apply several suggestions in one commit
### User Story

Labels: `enhancement`, `scope: medium` · Type: Feature · Part of #151 · Depends on #156 (S3, merged in #179), #157 (S4), #158 (S5) and #189 (S6a)

As a PR author, I want to pick several suggestions and apply them together so that my branch gets
one commit instead of one per suggestion.

### User Scenario

Ana leaves four suggestions on two files. Ben clicks **Add to batch** on three of them; a bar at the
bottom shows "3 suggestions selected · Apply". He applies them and the PR gets one commit changing
both files, and all three comments are marked applied.

### Acceptance Criteria

Errors from the batch Apply POST are returned as in S3 (#156): HTTP 400 with the message shown on
the page, unless an AC says otherwise. "Nothing is committed" means the head branch is unchanged
and no suggestion is marked applied.

- [ ] AC1: Given several selected suggestions, when applied, then one commit containing all of
  them is added and each is marked applied (S4) with that commit. The form is prefilled with
  "Apply <N> suggestions from code review" and can be edited, as in S3 AC1. Each reviewer other
  than the applier is credited as in S3 (customer question 1 default).
- [ ] AC2: Given two suggestions on the same file whose line ranges share a line (a single-line
  suggestion's range is its one line; a range suggestion's is S5's start–end), when the user tries
  to add the second to the batch, then it is refused with "overlaps another suggestion in this
  batch". A direct POST with both gets 400 with the same message and nothing is committed.
- [ ] AC3: Given one suggestion in the batch is outdated (S3 AC3, S6a AC3), when applied, then
  nothing is committed and the message is S3's "This suggestion is outdated: the code changed
  since it was written." followed by that suggestion's file and line (all or nothing).
- [ ] AC4: Given suggestions were added to the batch but not applied, when the page is reloaded,
  then no batch bar is shown and every suggestion shows **Add to batch** again (the batch is not
  stored server-side). Checked by an E2E test, since there is no server state to assert.
- [ ] AC5: Given a viewer who can't push to the head branch, then no suggestion shows **Add to
  batch**, and a direct POST returns 403 and commits nothing. A signed-out viewer sees no button,
  and a direct POST redirects to sign-in and commits nothing (S3 AC2).
- [ ] AC6: Given the PR is closed or merged, its head branch was deleted, or it uses AGit flow,
  then no **Add to batch** button is shown, and a direct POST returns 400 with "Suggestions can
  only be applied to an open pull request whose branch still exists." and commits nothing (S3
  AC5).
- [ ] AC7: Given the head branch moved since the page loaded, when the batch is applied with the
  old head SHA, then nothing is committed and they see "This branch has new commits since the
  page was loaded. Reload the page and try again." (S3 AC4).
- [ ] AC8: Given the head branch is protected against this user's push, when the batch is applied,
  then nothing is committed and they see `Cannot commit to protected branch "<branch>".` (S3 AC6).
- [ ] AC9: Given two suggestions in one file that change line counts differently (one replaces
  one line with three, one further down deletes its line), when applied together, then the
  committed file is the same as applying them one at a time, and no other line changes.
- [ ] AC10: Given an already-applied suggestion (S4), then it has no **Add to batch** button
  (S4 AC1), and a direct POST that includes it returns 400 with "This suggestion has already been
  applied." (S4 AC2) followed by its file and line, and commits nothing.
- [ ] AC11: Given a batch of one suggestion, when applied, then the commit's content and default
  message are the same as S3's **Apply suggestion** on that suggestion.
- [ ] AC12: Given an empty batch, then the batch bar is hidden. A direct POST with no suggestions
  returns 400 and commits nothing.
- [ ] AC13: Given a suggestion already in the batch, then its button reads **Remove from batch**,
  so it can't be added twice. A direct POST that lists the same suggestion twice returns 400 and
  commits nothing.
- [ ] AC14: Given a batch of 50 suggestions, when the user tries to add another, then it is
  refused with "A batch can hold at most 50 suggestions." A direct POST with 51 returns 400 with
  the same message and commits nothing.
- [ ] AC15: Given a range suggestion (S5) and a single-line suggestion in the same file that don't
  overlap, when both are applied in one batch, then the commit applies each exactly as S6a AC1 and
  S3 AC1 would on their own.

### Out of Scope

- Batches across PRs; saving a batch for later.
- Applying a single range suggestion on its own (S6a, #S6A).

### Open Questions

- ~~Is there a maximum batch size?~~ Resolved: 50 (AC14).

### Design Decision

**Decision:** Generalise S3's service to take a list of comment IDs and build one
`ChangeRepoFiles` call with one entry per file, applying edits in a file bottom-up so earlier
replacements don't shift later line numbers.

**Alternatives Considered:**
- *Apply each suggestion as its own commit in a loop.* Easy, but not atomic: a failure halfway
  leaves a partial result, and it is not what the user asked for.
- *Store pending batches server-side.* Survives reloads, but needs a table and cleanup for
  something the user does in one sitting.

**Rationale:** One `ChangeRepoFiles` call is a single atomic commit, and bottom-up edits are a
simple, testable way to avoid line drift.

**Consequences:** S3's function signature changes; S7's batch endpoint reuses it.

### Scope

medium

### Scope Justification

- **Service:** `services/repository/files/suggestion.go` takes a list of comments and runs S3's
  checks on each (S4's already-applied check, overlap, the limit), then applies S6a's range-aware
  edit per file bottom-up in one `ChangeRepoFiles` (AC1–AC3, AC9–AC15).
- **Web:** one route in `routers/web/web.go`, a handler in `routers/web/repo/pull_review.go`
  reusing S3's error mapping, and a form in `services/forms` (AC5–AC8).
- **Frontend:** **Add to batch** / **Remove from batch** and the batch bar in
  `web_src/js/markup/suggestion.ts`, with Vitest tests (AC2, AC12–AC14), plus a few locale strings.
- **Tests:** unit tests for line drift and overlap, integration tests for AC5–AC8 and AC10 sharing
  one PR setup, and one E2E test for AC4.
- No schema change. Medium fits: one service change, one UI bar, one commit.

---

| Criterion | Score (1–10) | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Correctness — implements issue requirements | 7 | AC1–AC14 work, and the bottom-up edits and per-file protected-branch check are right. AC15 isn't done but the PR closes #159 (1). A batch can get stuck on a deleted or edited comment (3). |
| Test coverage — tests present and meaningful | 9 | Every AC from AC1 to AC14 is tested at the service, handler and page level, and the 51-unparsable-IDs case is a nice way to prove the limit runs before lookups. Not covered: a batch holding a comment that was deleted or edited after it was added (3). |
| Test evidence — does every AC have a test? Are the expected values justified? Which tests did you run locally? | 9 | Each AC maps to named tests with its source, AC15 is explained, and the AI-written tests are listed. I ran the tests listed above. |
| Code quality — style, naming, no duplication | 8 | `ApplySuggestion` as a one-element call to `ApplySuggestions` keeps one code path, and `postApply` removes S3's duplicated POST code. One query per comment ID (6), and the template attributes are already noted under Tech Debt. |
| Documentation — comments and PR description clear | 9 | Clear description, Test Evidence, mutation write-up and an honest Tech Debt section. |
| AI transparency — evidence of human verification if AI used | 7 | The PR's AI section says what was AI-written and what you checked, but it points to "the AI Assistance comment on the linked issue", and #159 only has the one for the spec revision (2). |
| Overall — merge as-is? | 7 | Not yet. Fix 1–3 and it's ready. |

**Required**

1. **The PR closes #159, but AC15 isn't done.** The description says AC15 waits for #189 (still open), but `Closes #159` will close the issue on merge with AC15 unchecked and nothing tracking it except #189's own scope. Either change it to `Part of #159`, or move AC15 into #189 (or a linked follow-up) on the issue before merging. The issue body also still has `#S6A` placeholders where #189 belongs.
2. **AI Assistance comment for the implementation.** #159's only AI Assistance comment covers the spec revision (`2026-11-17_claude-code_issue-159-spec.md`). Please post one for this implementation's log so the PR's pointer leads somewhere.
3. **A deleted or edited comment gets stuck in the batch.** `batch` (`suggestion.ts:104`) is only changed by the toggle. Add A and B, then delete B, or edit B so it has no suggestion or two. The re-render shows no toggle for B, but B's ID is still in the batch. Every **Apply suggestions** then posts it, the server answers a bare 404 (comment not found, or `ErrSuggestionNotApplicable`), and the bar shows only "An error occurred". There's no way to remove B except reloading, and nothing tells the user that. Dropping entries whose element is gone when the bar is used (or when a comment re-renders without a toggle), or naming the suggestion on a 404 (see 5), would fix it. A Vitest case for this would go with the existing re-render test.

**Optional**

4. **`batch.values().some(...)` (`suggestion.ts:177`) needs Iterator helpers.** Iterator helpers are ES2025, the build targets es2020 (`vite.config.ts:74`) with no polyfill, and this is the first use in `web_src`. On Safari before 18.4 or Firefox before 131 it throws a `TypeError`, so a second suggestion can't be added. Vitest runs on Node, which has them, so the tests can't catch it. `[...batch.values()].some(...)` costs nothing.
5. **Some refusals still aren't named.** `ErrSuggestionNotApplicable` and a missing comment come back as a bare 404, and `ErrSuggestionOverlap` doesn't say which pair overlaps. For a batch of several, "An error occurred" leaves the user guessing which one to remove. Wrapping these in `ErrSuggestionAt` like the outdated and applied cases, and answering a JSON 400 for a batch, would match AC3/AC10's naming.
6. **One query per comment ID.** The handler calls `GetCommentByID` for each ID, and the service then loads each comment's review and poster one at a time, which is about 150 queries for a full batch of 50. One `db.Find` with `In("id", ids)` and `CommentList.LoadPosters` would cut that to a few. The limit-before-lookup check is a good guard either way.
7. **The ` (path:line)` suffix is appended after translation** (`pull_review.go:249`), so translators can't place or punctuate it. The plural-free "N suggestions selected" label is already under Tech Debt. A `%s` variant of the three named messages would fix this one the same way.

Generalising S3's service so single Apply runs through the same checks was the right call: S4's applied check and marking now cover both paths for free, and applying each file's edits bottom-up keeps line drift out of the picture.

— @vvchopra, review drafted with Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5); I read the diff and ran the tests listed above myself.

67	## Requirements & Design
68	
69	### Were specs complete before coding started?
70	
71	Yes, for every issue that was implemented. Each spec uses the course format (user story, bug report or hardening task) and got a "Spec reviewed" comment from a teammate before its PR was opened:
72	
73	- **#143–#145** were written and reviewed by controlled-opposition on Nov 5, the day #146 was opened.
74	- **The #151 sub-issues** were written on Nov 11. S1 and S2 were reviewed by CarsonRackley on Nov 11, and S3–S7 by controlled-opposition on Nov 11–12. S3 and S4 each got a second review after their revisions (#156 on Nov 12, #157 on Nov 17).
75	- **#118** kept its Sprint 2 spec and vvchopra's spec review from Oct 26.
76	- **#189 (S6a)**, split out of S6 on Nov 17 so that S6 could build on applying one multi-line suggestion, was reviewed by controlled-opposition the same day.
77	- **#181** was reviewed by ab-wm on Nov 15 (its AC7 target was measured and changed during review), **#186** by Jack-Donohue on Nov 17 and **#187** by vvchopra on Nov 17.
78	
79	**Surprises:**
80	
81	- **#151's open questions decided most of the design.** The feature issue asked who may apply a suggestion, who authors the commit, what happens when the code changed, and what happens on forks. Each answer became acceptance criteria spread across several sub-issues. S3's spec had to settle the commit author (the person who applies it, crediting the reviewer as co-author) before S4 could store who applied it.
82	- **The chain of dependencies.** S4 needed S3 merged (Nov 17), and S6 needs S3, S4, S5 and S6a (#189). That left the last links of the chain with little time.
83	- **Fixing CI exposed hidden failures.** Once #182 made `main` run every suite, flaky tests that PR runs had hidden started to show up on `main` (Suite health).
84	
85	### Key design decisions
86	
87	Every implemented issue records at least one decision with two or more alternatives in its issue body (D3). #143–#145 record theirs per commit, as #53 and #54 did in Sprint 1.
88	
89	- **#118:** The badge is a dot drawn on the existing favicon, reusing the code that already badges the icon with an Actions run's status, rather than a number in the icon or the page title. "Enable desktop notifications" is remembered in the browser rather than as a server setting.
90	- **#154 (S1):** The diff is drawn in the browser, the way Gitea already renders `mermaid` and `math` blocks. The server only adds the commented line from the comment's stored diff context.
91	- **#155 (S2):** The button reads the line text from the diff row already on the page. The code fence is one backtick longer than the longest run of backticks in the line, so any line can be quoted.
92	- **#156 (S3):** A new `ApplySuggestion` service next to `ChangeRepoFiles` refuses the commit if the head branch has moved since the page loaded, rather than merging the change in. The server only adds the Apply attributes for a viewer who may push, so the page never shows a button that would be refused.
93	- **#157 (S4):** Who applied a suggestion, and the commit, are stored in three new `comment` columns with defaults, so the migration is one `ALTER TABLE`, and a conditional `UPDATE` makes a second apply lose.
94	- **#158 (S5):** A range comment's start line is stored in the comment's existing metadata JSON, not in a new column. A range is marked outdated by comparing its lines' text, not by blame.
95	- **#143–#145:** ⬜ PENDING (ab-wm): one line on the main decision, e.g. where the "is this dependency resolved" rule lives.
96	- **#181:** The upstream release workflows are guarded with upstream's own `if: github.repository == 'go-gitea/gitea'`, rather than deleted or disabled in settings. Backend PRs got faster by refreshing the build cache and running the unit passes in parallel, not by dropping databases or `-race`.
97	- **#186:** Get a Playwright trace out of CI first, and fix the test only once the trace shows the cause, rather than adding waits blindly.

128	## Test Strategy
129	
130	Tests were written against each acceptance criterion, with expected values taken from the criteria, the issue discussion or upstream behaviour, never from the code's output. Each PR's Test Evidence table maps every AC to its test and says which tests AI wrote.
131	
132	- **Go unit tests** for models, services and handlers: #146, #149, #150, #168, #177, #179, #192, #193
133	- **Integration tests** through the full HTTP request path, on SQLite, MySQL, MSSQL and PostgreSQL in CI: #146, #149, #164, #168, #177, #179, #192, #193
134	- **Migration test:** #192 (S4's new `comment` columns)
135	- **Vitest** frontend unit tests: #150, #161, #162, #168, #175, #177, #179, #180, #192
136	- **Playwright end-to-end tests:** #150, #162, #177
137	- **CI only:** #182 and #191 change workflows, so their evidence is CI runs: throwaway draft PRs (#183, #184) before merge and the first runs on `main` after it.
138	
139	Mutation testing (D6) led to new tests: #175 for #118 and #180 for #155 each add a test that kills a surviving mutant.
140	
141	Changes we couldn't test automatically:
142	
143	- **Desktop notifications (#118):** the browser's permission prompt and the operating system's notification can't be driven in CI. The unit tests replace them, and #161's Test Evidence records a manual check in Chrome for each of them (AC3 to AC5).
144	- **The tab icon (#118):** the tests check which icon is chosen and when. What the dot looks like in a real tab was checked by hand in Chrome, as #161's Test Evidence records for AC1 and AC2.
145	- **What GitHub-style suggestions look like (#154, #156, #158):** layout was checked by hand with screenshots. The tests check the DOM.
146	- **CI timing (#181):** runner speed varies, so AC7's 22-minute median is measured on real runs rather than tested.
147	- ⬜ PENDING: anything from #159, #160 or #189.

168	### Failures, by cause
169	
170	- **Flaky, caused by our changes, Vitest:** the shortcut tests and the `r` quote-reply test (Sprint 2's #116) fail when Vitest puts `shortcut.test.ts` and `repo-issue-edit.test.ts` in the same worker, because `isolate: false` lets them share one `document`. It failed on `main` above and on #192's first run, and passes when the files land in different workers. Tracked in **#171**.
171	- **Flaky, caused by our changes, MSSQL:** S3's integration test failed once on MSSQL (`main`, run above). The comment it posts right after the previous Apply got a 500 after 1.9 s, while that Apply's push was still being processed. It passed on MSSQL in 14 other runs from Nov 13 to Nov 19, on #179, #177 and `main`. Tracked in **#195** (Sprint 4).
172	- **Flaky, caused by our changes, PostgreSQL:** `TestRepoCalendar` (Sprint 2's #123) fails under the race detector when the mocked clock is reset while an indexer worker reads it. Not in the two runs above. Tracked in **#185**.
173	- **Flaky, e2e:** "repo topics can be added and removed by keyboard" failed in CI Chromium on Nov 15 (#183, #184). It passed in both runs above. **#186** now keeps a trace of any failed e2e test so the cause can be found.
174	- **Environment-specific:** at the s2 tag, the CI Vitest job stops with `Cannot find dependency '@vitest/coverage-v8'`, because that package was added after s2 (#141). The baseline was run locally instead (`pnpm exec vitest run` at `40e0aa79`, Debian WSL). Recorded in **#181**, Decision 4.
175	
176	No test the team added this sprint is skipped. The 3 skipped Playwright tests were skipped at s2 too, each with a reason in a code comment: two WebKit Tab-order skips (`aria-menu.test.ts:44`, `menus.test.ts:54`) and an upstream Firefox skip (`file-view-render.test.ts:6`). ⬜ PENDING: an issue link for the two WebKit skips, which come from our Sprint 1 `<aria-menu>` work. The only CI change that turns something off is #182's skip of upstream's release workflows, which links #181 in a same-line comment on every job.

283	## Risks and Retrospective
284	
285	### What worked
286	
287	- **Splitting #151 along its dependencies.** S1 merged on Nov 12, the day after the split, so S2, S3 and S5 could be built on it in parallel.
288	- **Spec reviews that settled the hard questions first.** S3's two reviews settled who authors the commit, what "outdated" means and how forks behave before any code was written. Its PR review then found edge cases (an archived fork, a line above the comment that changed) rather than design problems.
289	- **Mutation testing found real gaps.** It showed new lines that ran under tests but whose results no test checked. #175 and #180 added tests that kill those survivors.
290	- **Fixing CI.** After #182, `main` runs every suite on every merge, and the s2 tag could be tested for the baseline. That is why this report has a Suite health table, and why the flaky tests above were found.
291	
292	### What slowed the team down
293	
294	- **The feature was split late.** #151 was posted on Nov 7, and the sub-issues were written on Nov 11, eight days into a seventeen-day sprint. Our Sprint 2 goal was to write and review every spec in the first three days.
295	- **The end of the chain ran out of time.** S4 couldn't start its PR until S3 merged on Nov 17, so it merged on the last day, and S6 depends on four other issues. #187 (S8) carries over. ⬜ PENDING: which of #159, #160 and #189 do too.
296	- **Review load.** ab-wm reviewed 6 of the 14 code PRs, controlled-opposition 3, CarsonRackley 3 and vvchopra and Jack-Donohue 1 each. Our Sprint 2 goal was at least two reviews per member.
297	- **A wrong merge.** #163 (S1) was merged by mistake while another PR was meant, then reverted (#166) and merged again as #168, all on Nov 12.
298	- **Flaky tests.** Until #182, `main` didn't run the integration and e2e suites, and its status was red anyway, so flaky failures were noticed late.
299	
300	### Changes for Sprint 4
301	
302	- Split the team feature into sub-issues, and write and review their specs, within the first three days.
303	- When one issue blocks another, merge the blocking PR by mid-sprint. Otherwise move the blocked issue out at planning time instead of on the last day.
304	- Name a reviewer when each PR is opened, rotating so that every member reviews at least two PRs.
305	- Treat a red `main` as a stop: whoever's merge turned it red fixes it or files an issue that day.
306	
307	## Sprint 4 Plan
308	
309	Carryover issues:
310	
311	- #187 (S8, controlled-opposition): the "Suggest change" button in reply forms. Its spec is reviewed and it builds only on S2, so it can start on day one.
312	- ⬜ PENDING: whichever of #159 (S6), #160 (S7) and #189 (S6a) are not merged by the deadline.
313	- #171 (flaky Vitest pairing) and #185 (`TestRepoCalendar` data race), plus #195 (the MSSQL flake in S3's integration test).
314	- #101 and #102, the private and personal calendar feeds, if the team takes them.
315	
316	Initial ideas, from this sprint's Tech Debt sections:
317	
318	- Stop computing the Apply check on every page that renders code comments, and add it where "Expand" reveals more of a file (#179, and the #192 review).
319	- Refuse an outdated suggestion less often: S3 compares the lines above the comment, which can refuse a suggestion whose own line is unchanged (#179).
320	- Ask the TA to make the combined CI check required and to protect tags, which needs admin rights (#181).

Course rules, not upstream Gitea ones. Source: the course site <https://csci-435-se.github.io/>
(Sprints pages and Glossary) and `docs/sprint0/standards.md`. Everyone on the team, and every AI
session, uses the formats below so all issues and PRs look the same. The GitHub templates in
`.github/` carry the same formats; if they ever disagree with this page, fix the template.

AI disclosure has its own page: `AI-ASSISTANCE.md`.

## Current sprint: Sprint 3

- **Dates:** Nov 3 – Nov 19, 2026. Everything pushed and merged by **Nov 19, 11:59 PM**, except
  the D7 check-in, due **Nov 12, 11:59 PM** together with at least one code PR of your own, open
  and ready for review or merged.
- **Focus:** testing, meaning how well the tests check what the code is supposed to do.

- **Zero rule:** no merged PR (D4), no sprint report (D8) or no release (D9) means **0 for the
  whole sprint**.
- **Carries forward:** anything the Sprint 3 page doesn't change comes from the Sprint 2 and
  Sprint 1 pages, and every Sprint 0 standard still applies.
- **Start early:** record the test baseline at the Sprint 2 tag (see D8), and get the mutation tool

### Graded strictly this sprint

The Sprint 3 page lists these as the rules that cost the most points. Details are in the sections
named.
  go-mutesting: save the terminal output to a text file. The scores in the write-up must match the
  reports, and the mutant your new test kills must show as killed in the "after" report.
- The tool configuration you used, committed and linked from the write-up. Reusing a teammate's
  setup is encouraged, as long as you run the tool yourself and credit them. The team's shared
  setup (go-mutesting for Go), its commands and its pitfalls: `.claude-students/docs/mutation-testing.md`.

Common problems:

- **The tool stops before mutating.** It first runs the selected tests on unchanged code and stops
  if any fail. Fix or exclude them first; the D8 baseline shows which ones fail already.
- **Tests run against built code.** Mutants in the source are never seen by tests that run on
  compiled output. Configure a rebuild, or pick tests that run on source.
- **Tests need services.** Start the database or service first. How each test type runs is in
  `.claude-students/docs/testing.md`.
- **False survivors.** When limiting which tests run, include the tests that cover the mutated
  files. Otherwise mutants they would catch show as survived or not covered. Check that the
  relevant tests ran before writing a new test for a survivor.
- **Blocked?** Ask teammates first. Then tell the TA **as early as possible**, with the errors and
  the AI log of what you tried; the TA may approve a different issue or area. Problems reported at
  the end of the sprint don't excuse a missing D6.

Template, copied from the Sprint 3 page:

```markdown
# Mutation testing: Issue #<N> -- <issue title>

**PR(s):** #...  **Tool:** ...  **Config:** [link; credit the teammate if you reused their setup]  **Command:** `...`
**Reports:** [before](reports/<issue#>-<username>-before.json) · [after](reports/<issue#>-<username>-after.json)
**Mutation score:** before ...% → after ...%

## Surviving mutants

| Location (file:line) | Mutation | Equivalent or test gap? | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| | | | |

## New or strengthened test

Commit: [link] · Test: [file › test name] · Kills: [mutant location]

## Questions

1. What did the surviving mutants reveal about your tests?
2. Did any surviving mutant point to an assertion whose expected value was not based on the requirements? Explain.
3. If you used AI to configure the tool, analyze survivors, or write tests, what did it produce and what did you verify or correct? If AI was not used, write "N/A."
```

Grading (15 points): tool run on the files changed by the PR, with configuration, command, results
and reports committed 4; surviving mutants analysed correctly (equivalent or test gap, with an
explanation) 4; at least one new or strengthened test kills a survivor, confirmed by the re-run 4;
answers show understanding, not just description 3. CSCI 535: the average of the two write-ups.

## Sprint report (D8) sections

`docs/sprint<N>/report.md` (or `.pdf` or `.docx`), following `docs/sprint0/report.md`:

- Team: names, GitHub usernames, project name, repository link.
- Sprint overview.
- Backlog: milestone link, why the team chose these issues, plus a table of title, owner, points,
  scope and status.
- Requirements and design: when specs were done, what surprised you, design rationale.
- Completed issues: title, owner, PR link, author, reviewer, what changed.
- Test strategy, including untestable changes and why.
- AI tool usage per member: tools, session count, AI log folder link, and 2–3 sentences on lessons
  learned.
- Release: tag and release link.
- Risks and retrospective: what worked, what slowed the team down, next-sprint changes.
- Next sprint plan: initial ideas and carryover issues.
- New in Sprint 3:
  - **Suite health** (keep it short). A baseline table of the test suites relevant to the team (the
    packages or areas it works on, not the whole repository): for each suite, the command or CI
    workflow and the runner's summary line (passed, failed, skipped) at the Sprint 2 tag
    `v1.27.3-csci435-s2` and at the end of the sprint. Use CI results where available; locally, run
    only the packages you change. Failures are grouped by cause (e.g. environment-specific, already
    broken upstream, flaky, caused by our changes), each cause linking one issue that lists the
    affected tests. Any test the team's changes broke is fixed by the end of the sprint;
    pre-existing failures only need recording and grouping. Every skipped test and disabled CI
    check has a linked issue and a reason in a code comment.
  - **Mutation testing:** a link to each member's D6 write-up.
  - **Hardening issues:** which issues they are and where they came from.
  - **Carryovers:** the Sprint 2 issues carried over, and what changed.
- The report covers this sprint's work only. Write the Sprint 3 sections fresh rather than copying
  a previous report, and check that tables and links render on GitHub (no escaped `\|` or `\[`).

## Test Evidence
levels: ['CI', 'integration', 'unit']
## Test Evidence


Each refusal test also checks that the head branch didn't move, i.e. "commits nothing".

**Not tested automatically, and why:** None.

**Mutation testing (D6):** [`docs/sprint3/mutation/160-arjunsb26.md`](docs/sprint3/mutation/160-arjunsb26.md). go-mutesting on the functions this PR changed: 41.3% → 57.1%. The new unit test kills the ten error-mapping survivors.

**AI-written tests:** Claude Code wrote `TestAPIPullReviewApplySuggestion` and
`TestApplyPullReviewSuggestionError`, and changed
`services/repository/files/suggestion_test.go` (a mechanical change: an `errOf` helper drops the
new SHA return value, and no expected values changed). I checked each status code and the default
message against the revised ACs and #156 AC1, not against the code's output.

## Design

See the Design Decision on #160: no create endpoint, one apply endpoint over S3's service, and
status codes that follow the file API.


## Tech Debt

**Introduced:** `getPullReviewCommentToResolve` is reused to load the comment for apply, so its
name no longer fits. I left it alone to keep the diff small. The pending-review check is done in
both the handler (to answer 404) and the service (which returns not-applicable).

**Encountered:** The UI's apply endpoint answers almost every refusal with 400 and a localized
message, so the API maps the same service errors to statuses separately. A later change could
move the mapping next to the service errors.


######## PR 198 first line: Closes #187
## Test Evidence
levels: ['E2E', 'E2E, unit', 'unit', 'unit, E2E']
## Test Evidence


**Not tested automatically, and why:** Quote reply opening the form (AC1) isn't driven separately; Files tab Quote reply calls the same `handleReply` (`repo-issue-edit.ts`), so it gets the same setup. Resolved conversations (AC1) aren't driven either; expanding one only shows the same reply form.

**AI-written tests:** Claude Code wrote all of them: the five `initReplySuggestChangeButton` unit tests, the `handleReply` unit test, the two new E2E tests, the AC8 step in the range test, and the change to S2's reply assertion. I checked the expected blocks against #155's ACs. Breaking the code made them fail: dropping the side check failed the AC2 unit test, and setting up the button on every Reply failed the AC4 E2E step with a second block.

**AI-changed existing tests:** Claude Code made two more test changes so the suite passes reliably with the new `handleReply` test. Only the first touches a test from outside #187:
- `r quotes the selection after the existing text, or only moves to the reply box` (#95, `repo-issue-edit.test.ts`): its three `r` key presses are now `cancelable: true`, like a real key press. When `shortcut.test.ts` and this file shared a worker, each press reached two global listeners. A non-cancelable event got past the `defaultPrevented` check, so the quote ran twice. The expected values didn't change.
- The `handleReply` test imports `repo-issue.ts` between two `vi.resetModules()` calls. Otherwise its copy of `repo-diff-range.ts`, loaded w

## Design

As in the issue's Design Decision. One change during implementation: the spec's test plan put AC4 in Vitest. A unit test of `handleReply` has to mock `ComboMarkdownEditor`. In a separate file it clashed with `repo-issue-edit.test.ts`'s mock under `isolate: false` (about 2 of 5 full runs), so AC4 went to E2E against the real editor. SonarQube then flagged `handleReply` as uncovered new code, so a unit test for it now lives in `repo-issue-edit.test.ts`, which already owns that mock.


## Tech Debt

**Introduced:** Each new E2E test takes 6–8 s per browser, over the 2 s target, mostly in creating the repo and PR through the API. Grouping them would share setup but make each one check several things.

**Encountered:** `vitest.config.ts` runs files with `isolate: false` and tests concurrently, so two test files can't safely mock the same module with different factories, and a test that `await`s while using `document.body` can be cleared by another test's `beforeEach`. Two test files that both call `initGlobalShortcut()` also add duplicate document listeners when they share a worker. I worked around all three in the tests and left the config as is.

This is the D6 mutation testing deliverable for #158, whose PR #177 is already merged, so this PR doesn't close the issue. It changes no product code.

- Four new tests, each killing a surviving mutant that showed a gap:
  - `repo-diff-range.test.ts`: a range that spans an existing comment thread (without the `?.` that would throw), a two-line range, and a new→old shift-click being refused (AC11, "or the other way round").
  - `repo-diff-suggestion.test.ts`: Suggest change on a CRLF line drops the whole line ending (AC4).
- Write-up: [`docs/sprint3/mutation/158-Jack-Donohue.md`](docs/sprint3/mutation/158-Jack-Donohue.md), with the before and after reports and my Stryker config (`Jack-Donohue.stryker.config.mjs`, following vvchopra's and ab-wm's pattern).

Score: 72.58% → 75.81% (covered code: 91.84% → 95.92%). The remaining 4 survivors are 3 equivalent mutants and 1 rare edge case, explained in the write-up.


## Why

D6 needs a mutation-testing write-up for one of my issues (two for CSCI 535). #177 merged without one.


## Test Evidence
levels: ['unit']
## Test Evidence


**Not tested automatically, and why:** N/A. Every change is a test.

**AI-written tests:** Claude Code wrote all four tests. Each passed on the unchanged source before the after run, and each one's mutant shows as killed in the after report. I checked each expected value against the AC it cites.

## CI / manual verification

- `pnpm exec vitest run web_src/js/features/repo-diff-range.test.ts web_src/js/features/repo-diff-suggestion.test.ts`: 19 passed.
- StrykerJS before and after runs (the command is in the write-up): before 90 killed, 8 survived, 26 not covered; after 94 killed, 4 survived. The reports are in `docs/sprint3/mutation/reports/`.
- CI: `frontend` and `test-frontend-coverage` can fail on `repo-issue-edit.test.ts:78`, the known flake in #171, which this PR doesn't touch. A re-run clears it.


## Design

**Decision:** Run StrykerJS on #177's TypeScript lines only.

**Alternatives considered:**
- *go-mutesting on #177's Go changes* (`services/pull/review.go`, `models/issues`). It mutates whole files and re-runs each package's database-backed tests for every mutant, which takes hours, and those changes already have unit and integration tests.
- *StrykerJS on the five whole files.* Faster than Go, but most of `repo-issue.ts` and `repo-diff.ts` isn't #177's code, so its survivors would say nothing about #177's tests.

**Rationale:** The range selection is #177's own logic and runs in about 40 seconds, so the before and after runs fit the sprint.

**Consequences:** The Go side has no mutation score. #177's wiring in `repo-issue.ts` and `repo-diff.ts` shows as uncovered, since only E2E tests run it.


## Tech Debt

**Introduced:** None.

**Encountered:**

- The comment form's error toast in `repo-diff.ts` and the range wiring in `repo-issue.ts` have no Vitest tests; only the E2E test covers them, so Stryker reports their 26 mutants as uncovered.
- The `/[\r\n]+$/` → `/[\r\n]+/` survivor in `repo-diff-suggestion.ts` differs only for a line with a bare `\r` before its end. It's recorded in the write-up, not fixed.

##### 160


**Decision:** No new create endpoint: suggestions stay markdown in the comment body. Add one apply
endpoint, `POST /repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/comments/{id}/suggestion/apply`, that takes `head_sha`
and an optional `message` and calls S3's service.

**Alternatives Considered:**
- *A structured create endpoint (`path`, `lines`, `replacement`).* Easier for bots, but two ways to
  author the same thing that must render identically.
- *Mirror GitHub's API shape exactly.* GitHub has no apply endpoint to mirror.

**Rationale:** Bots already post review comments through the existing API, so they get
suggestions for free, and the service layer is shared with the UI.

**Consequences:** New route and swagger entry (`docs/routers-api-v1.md`), new request and response
structs (`docs/modules-structs.md`). S3's service now returns the new commit's SHA.

**Decision 2 (status codes):** Refusals follow the existing file API (`PUT /contents`): branch
protection, protected files and pre-receive hook rejections are 403, like a missing push
permission. 409 means the pull request or the code moved on (stale `head_sha`, outdated line,
closed PR), and 422 means the comment has nothing to apply.

##### 187

# AI Logs

This folder holds every AI session for each sprint, one folder per student. The course rules are on
the [AI Log Instructions](https://csci-435-se.github.io/ai-logs/) page and the current sprint page
at <https://csci-435-se.github.io/>. This README is the team's shared convention for following them.

## What to log

Every AI session tied to this project: code, debugging, tests, reviews, drafting issues and PRs,
design discussion, the sprint report. That includes sessions that went nowhere. Purely academic
questions unrelated to the project don't need logging.

## Structure

```
ai-logs/
  sprint<N>/
    <github-username>/                          ← exact GitHub username, matching case
      .gitkeep                                  ← the folder must exist even if you used no AI
      YYYY-MM-DD_<tool>_<short-slug>.md
      YYYY-MM-DD_<tool>_<short-slug>/           ← attachments (images, etc.), optional
```

Team folders: `ab-wm`, `arjunsb26`, `CarsonRackley`, `controlled-opposition`, `Jack-Donohue`,
`vvchopra`.

## Naming

`YYYY-MM-DD_<tool>_<short-slug>.md`

- **Date:** the day the session started.
- **Sprint folder:** the sprint that date falls in, not the sprint the work is for.
- **Tool:** one of the course identifiers: `claude-code`, `claude-web`, `claude-desktop`, `cursor`,
  `gemini-cli`, `codex-cli`, `copilot`, `chatgpt`, `other-<name>`. Claude Code run inside VS Code is
  `claude-code`.
- **Slug:** lowercase words joined with hyphens that say what the session did. Put the issue number
  first when there is one: `issue-52-impl`, `issue-52-spec`, `pr-61-review`, `sprint1-report`.
  Replace auto-generated slugs such as `local-command-caveat...`.
- **Formats:** `.md` is preferred; `.txt` and `.json` are also accepted. No `.docx`, `.pdf`, `.html`
  or share links.

## Capturing a session

| Tool | How |
| --- | --- |
| Claude Code (terminal or VS Code), other agentic CLIs | Start it with [SpecStory](https://specstory.com/): `specstory run claude`, from the repo root. Forgot? Run `specstory sync` afterwards; it back-fills from Claude Code's local history. Then copy from `.specstory/history/` (git-ignored) into your folder and rename it to the convention. |
| Web chat (claude.ai, ChatGPT, Gemini, ...) | Install a browser chat exporter and export the session as Markdown right after it ends. Include any files you pasted in as context. |
| Claude Desktop | SpecStory doesn't capture it. Copy the conversation into a `.md` file by hand. |

At the end of each sprint, run `specstory sync` once more and re-copy. A log copied mid-session is
incomplete.

## Content

- The **tool and AI model** used (SpecStory writes both).
- The **complete** prompt and response history. For agentic tools, that includes file edits and
  commands (SpecStory includes them). Logs with missing responses or truncated histories are
  **invalid**. Don't hand-write, summarise or trim a log; only rename it.
- These are **not** logs and get no full credit: a summary of a session, paraphrased prompts, a
  share link to a chat, or tool output without the prompts that produced it (Sprint 3 page).
- Attachments (screenshots, snippets) go in a folder with the log's name minus `.md`.
- Log **every** session, including ones that went nowhere. Grading is on how complete the record
  is, not on whether AI helped.

## Where logs are referenced

- **Issue comments only.** Each contributor posts their own `### AI Assistance — @username` comment
  on the issue, with full `https://github.com/...` links to their logs. Format:
  [`.claude-students/AI-ASSISTANCE.md`](../.claude-students/AI-ASSISTANCE.md).
- **Not** in PR descriptions or PR comments. The PR has a short AI-use note with no log link. The
  AI Log Instructions page says "Issue/PR comments" and the Sprint 3 page "the issue or PR", but
  the Sprint 1 page narrows it to issue comments only; the team keeps that rule, which satisfies
  all three.
- Each teammate posts their own comment, including reviewers who used AI to review.
- No AI used? Post an issue comment saying so, and keep your folder with its `.gitkeep`.
- The sprint report lists each member's tools, session count, folder link, and 2–3 sentences on
  lessons learned.
```

305	## What changed
306	
307	A suggestion on a range of lines (S5, #158) can now be applied like a single-line one, on its own
308	or in a batch (S6, #159).
309	
310	- **Service (`services/repository/files/suggestion.go`):**
311	  - Removed the guard that refused range comments until this issue.
312	  - `applySuggestionToContent` keeps its signature. `original` can now hold several lines joined
313	    by `"\n"`: the range ends at `lineNum`, and its start is that minus the line count, as #159's
314	    `suggestionEdit.startLine()` already worked it out.
315	  - One loop checks the lines above the range and every line in it, then replaces them all.
316	  - The last line of the range sets the line ending, so a range that ends on a last line with no
317	    final newline keeps the file ending without one.
318	- **Model (`models/issues/comment_suggestion.go`):** for a range, `SuggestionContextLines()` drops
319	  the range's own lines, which would otherwise be checked twice, once as context and once as the
320	  original. It also keeps only the last `CODE_COMMENT_LINES` lines above L, the same number S3
321	  checks. S5 stores a range's whole hunk, so without the cap an unrelated in-place edit far up the
322	  hunk would make the suggestion outdated.
323	- **API:** S7's `POST …/comments/{id}/apply` (#160) calls the same service, so it applies ranges
324	  too, with no change to the API.
325	- **Templates:** removed `(not .RangeStartLine)` from the Apply condition in `diff/comments.tmpl`
326	  and `issue/view_content/conversation.tmpl`. Range suggestions now get Apply, and with it
327	  **Add to batch**.
328	- No route, JS, locale or schema change. The batch frontend and the overlap check already handled
329	  ranges.

func (c *Comment) RangeOriginalLines() ([]string, bool) {
	start := c.RangeStartLine()
	if start <= 0 || c.Line < start {
		return nil, false
	}
	return PatchLastNewLines(c.Patch, int(c.Line-start+1))
}

// PatchLastNewLines returns the last n new-side lines of a one-hunk patch, which end at the
// commented line, skipping removed lines. False if the hunk has fewer than n.
func PatchLastNewLines(patch string, n int) ([]string, bool) {
	rows := strings.Split(strings.TrimRight(patch, "\n"), "\n")
	lines := make([]string, n)
	for i := len(rows) - 1; i >= 0 && n > 0; i-- {
		switch {
		case rows[i] == "" || rows[i][0] == '@':
			return nil, false // reached the hunk header
		case rows[i][0] == '+' || rows[i][0] == ' ':
			n--
			lines[n] = rows[i][1:]
		}
	}
	return lines, n == 0
}

// SuggestionContextLines returns the new-side lines the stored patch shows above the commented line, or above a
// multi-line comment's first line, in file order. Applying a suggestion checks them too, since blame-based invalidation can miss the commented line
// moving onto an identical one, like another "}" (#156 AC3).
func (c *Comment) SuggestionContextLines() []string {
	if !c.SuggestionOriginalLine().Has() {
		return nil
	}
	lines := strings.Split(strings.TrimRight(c.Patch, "\n"), "\n")
	hunkStart := -1
	for i, line := range lines {
		if strings.HasPrefix(line, "@@") {
			hunkStart = i
		}
	}
	if hunkStart < 0 {
		return nil
	}
	var above []string
	for _, line := range lines[hunkStart+1 : len(lines)-1] { // the last line is the commented one
		if line != "" && (line[0] == ' ' || line[0] == '+') {
			above = append(above, line[1:])
		} // "-" is the old side, "\" is "No newline at end of file"
	}
	if start := c.RangeStartLine(); start > 0 {
		above = above[:len(above)-int(c.Line-start)] // a range's own lines aren't context; SuggestionOriginalLine holds them (#189)
		// a range stores its whole hunk; check only as many lines above as a single-line comment's snippet holds
		above = above[max(0, len(above)-setting.UI.CodeCommentLines):]
	}
	return above
}

// CutDiffAroundLine cuts a diff of a file in way that only the given line + numberOfLine above it will be shown
// it also recalculates hunks and adds the appropriate headers to the new diff.
// Warning: Only one-file diffs are allowed.
func CutDiffAroundLine(originalDiff io.Reader, line int64, old bool, numbersOfLine int) (string, error) {
	if line == 0 || numbersOfLine == 0 {
		// no line or num of lines => no diff
		return "", nil
	}

	scanner := bufio.NewScanner(originalDiff)
	hunk := make([]string, 0)

	// begin is the start of the hunk containing searched line
	// end is the end of the hunk ...
	// currentLine is the line number on the side of the searched line (differentiated by old)
	// otherLine is the line number on the opposite side of the searched line (differentiated by old)
	var begin, end, currentLine, otherLine int64
	var headerLines int

	inHunk := false

	for scanner.Scan() {
		lof := scanner.Text()
		// Add header to enable parsing

		if isHeader(lof, inHunk) {
			if strings.HasPrefix(lof, cmdDiffHead) {
				inHunk = false
			}
			hunk = append(hunk, lof)
			headerLines++
		}
		if currentLine > line {
			break
		}
		// Detect "hunk" with contains commented lof
		if strings.HasPrefix(lof, "@@") {
			inHunk = true
			// Already got our hunk. End of hunk detected!
			if len(hunk) > headerLines {
				break
			}
			// A map with named groups of our regex to recognize them later more easily

### Acceptance Criteria

Errors from the Apply POST are returned as in S3 (#156): HTTP 400 with the message shown on the
page, unless an AC says otherwise.

- [ ] AC1: Given a suggestion on lines L–M (S5) and a user who can push to the head branch, when
  they apply it, then exactly one commit is added that replaces lines L–M with the block's lines
  in order, matching S5 AC5's diff. No line before L or after M changes. The commit message
  follows S3 AC1 (default "Apply suggestion from @<reviewer> on <file>", editable).
- [ ] AC2: Given the block is empty or holds one blank line, when it is applied, then the commit
  deletes lines L–M, or replaces them with one blank line (S5 AC6, S3 AC12).
- [ ] AC3: Given any line in L–M (first, middle or last) differs at head from the line the
  suggestion was written against, or one of the lines S3 checks above the commented line
  (`[ui] CODE_COMMENT_LINES`, 4 by default) now differs above L (S3's check for code that moved
  onto identical text, like another `}`), or the file now has fewer than M
  lines, or it was deleted or renamed, when someone applies it, then nothing is committed and they
  see "This suggestion is outdated: the code changed since it was written."
- [ ] AC4: Given a range suggestion, then the Apply button is shown or hidden under the same
  conditions as a single-line one (S3 AC2, AC5, AC7, AC9), and a direct POST gets S3's responses:
  403 for a user who can't push, 400 "Suggestions can only be applied to an open pull request
  whose branch still exists." for a closed or merged PR, 400 "This branch has new commits since
  the page was loaded. Reload the page and try again." for a stale head, and `Cannot commit to
  protected branch "<branch>".` for a protected branch.
- [ ] AC5: Given a file with CRLF line endings or no final newline, including a range that ends
  on the last line, when a range suggestion is applied, then the new lines use the file's line
  ending and the file's final-newline state is unchanged (S3 AC11).
- [ ] AC6: Given a range suggestion whose block equals lines L–M, when applied, then nothing is
  committed and they see "This suggestion makes no changes to the code." (S3 AC10).
- [ ] AC7: Given a single-line suggestion, then applying it behaves exactly as before: S3's
  `TestApplySuggestionToContent` cases keep their inputs, expected results and call unchanged and
  pass, as do S3's other tests. *Reworded after the spec review.*
- [ ] AC8: Given a range suggestion and a single-line suggestion in the same file that don't overlap, when both are applied in one batch (S6, #159), then the commit applies each exactly as AC1 and S3 AC1 would on their own. *Moved from #159 AC15.*
- [ ] AC9: Given a range comment whose original lines can't be read back from its stored snippet
  (S5's `RangeOriginalLines()` returns false), then no Apply button is shown, and a direct POST
  gets 404, as S3 AC7 does for a comment with no applicable suggestion. *Added after the spec
  review.*
- [ ] AC10: Given a suggestion posted as a reply in a range thread on lines L–M (S5 makes the
  reply inherit the range), when it is applied, then it replaces lines L–M, as AC1 does. *Added
  after the spec review.*

### Out of Scope

- Applying several suggestions in one commit (S6, #159), which reuses this.
- Recording "applied" (S4, #157) and the API (S7, #160).
- Re-anchoring a range whose lines moved but didn't change: it is refused as outdated, like S3.

### Open Questions

- None.

### Design Decision

**Decision:** Generalise S3's `applySuggestionToContent` in
`services/repository/files/suggestion.go` to replace the lines that end at `lineNum` and number
as many as the original has, keeping its signature. A range comment passes S5's
`SuggestionOriginalLine()`, which already joins lines L–M with `"\n"`. Every one of those lines,
plus the lines above L, is checked before replacing. For a range, `SuggestionContextLines()`
returns only the `CODE_COMMENT_LINES` lines above L. It leaves out the range's own lines, and
S5's stored snippet holds the whole hunk, so it caps the lines to as many as S3 checks.

**Alternatives Considered:**
- *An explicit start-line parameter on `applySuggestionToContent`.* Clearer at the call site, but
  every S3 test call would change. That is the conflict the spec review raised against AC7. S6
  already infers a range's start from the original's line count (`suggestionEdit.startLine()`), so
  a second source for the same number could disagree with it.
- *A separate `applyRangeSuggestionToContent`.* Leaves S3's function untouched, but duplicates its
  CRLF, final-newline and outdated handling, so the two would drift apart.
- *Build a patch from S5's rendered diff and run `git apply` in a temp clone.* S3 already rejected
  this: fuzzy matching can land the change on the wrong lines, and it duplicates what
  `ChangeRepoFiles` does.

**Rationale:** One function keeps a single place for line-ending handling. An unchanged signature
lets S3's tests serve as the single-line regression check (AC7) without editing them, and the
range's start comes from the same place S6's overlap check already reads it.

**Consequences:** S6

1. **The cap is one line wider than S3's check.** S3's single-line snippet comes from `CutDiffAroundLine(..., CODE_COMMENT_LINES)`, which keeps `CODE_COMMENT_LINES` rows *including* the commented line, so S3 checks at most 3 lines above it by default (`TestCutDiffAroundLine` shows 3 rows for `numbersOfLine` 3). A range now checks the 4 lines above L. It follows #189 AC3's wording ("4 by default"), so it isn't wrong against the spec, but the PR description and the `SuggestionContextLines` comment say it's "the same number S3 checks". Either use `CODE_COMMENT_LINES - 1` to match S3, or reword the comment so the next reader doesn't rely on them matching.
2. **Range Apply through the batch and API endpoints has no integration test.** AC8 is covered by `TestApplySuggestionsToContent` and the PR says S7's endpoint needs no change, which the code bears out. One range ID in `TestPullReviewApplySuggestions`, or one range comment in `TestAPIPullReviewApplySuggestion`, would prove it end to end. A follow-up is fine.
3. **Doc comment line length.** The second line of the `SuggestionContextLines` comment runs to about 150 characters, while the rest of the file wraps at 120. Rewrapping it would keep the file consistent.

Splitting S6a out of S6 and building it on S6's `startLine()` paid off: ranges went into the batch and its overlap check with no frontend change at all.

— @vvchopra, review drafted with Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5); I read the diff and ran the tests listed above myself.
